items.passage: As freshwater becomes scarcer, more countries are turning to the sea. Desalination plants remove salt from seawater, producing drinking water for cities that have run out of other sources. The technology is proven: Israel now gets more than half its domestic water from desalination, and large plants operate in Saudi Arabia, Australia and California. The main obstacle is cost. Desalination uses large amounts of energy, and the water it produces is usually more expensive than water from rivers or underground aquifers. A second problem is the brine left behind. For every litre of fresh water, a plant produces about one and a half litres of brine, water twice as salty as the sea, which is usually pumped back into the ocean. If the brine is released too close to shore, it can damage marine life on the seabed. Engineers are working on both problems. Solar-powered plants are being tested in the Middle East, and researchers are finding uses for brine, from extracting minerals to producing salt for industry. Supporters argue that desalination is the only reliable answer for coastal cities facing long droughts. Critics reply that it encourages wasteful use of water, since a city that can make its own water has less reason to fix leaks or use water carefully. The fairest view is that desalination is a valuable backup, but it works best in places that also manage demand, repair pipes, and reuse wastewater.

items.passage: For decades, night trains across Europe were in decline. Budget airlines offered cheaper and faster journeys, and railway companies found sleeper carriages expensive to run. By 2016, several countries had cancelled their last overnight services. Then the trend reversed. A new generation of travellers, concerned about the carbon emissions of flying, began to look for alternatives, and the night train offered something a plane could not: a bed, a slow journey through the landscape, and arrival in the city centre in the morning. The Austrian railway company led the revival, expanding its Nightjet network to connect Vienna with cities such as Amsterdam, Rome and Paris. Other operators followed, and new routes are now announced almost every year. The economics remain difficult. A sleeper train carries fewer passengers than a daytime train, and the carriages need staff through the night. Ticket prices are often higher than a budget flight, though supporters point out that the fare includes a night of accommodation. The revival also depends on infrastructure: border crossings, track maintenance and the availability of sleeper carriages all limit how fast the network can grow. Even so, the return of the night train shows how quickly a transport habit can change when travellers weigh comfort and climate alongside price, and when a railway company is willing to invest in a service that had been written off.

items.passage: In a concrete building on a Norwegian island, more than a million seed samples sit in frozen vaults. The Svalbard Global Seed Vault was built to protect the world's crop diversity against war, disaster and climate change. If a seed bank in a war zone is destroyed, or a crop variety is lost to drought, copies stored in Svalbard can be used to rebuild it. The idea is simple, but its importance is growing. Modern farming relies on a small number of high-yielding varieties, and thousands of traditional varieties have already disappeared. Those lost varieties may carry genes for drought resistance, disease resistance, or tolerance to salty soil, traits that could become vital as the climate changes. Critics of the vault argue that storing seeds is not enough. Seeds in a vault do not evolve with changing pests and diseases, while seeds grown by farmers adapt each season. Supporters reply that the vault is a backup, not a replacement for farming. Its purpose is to ensure that no variety is lost forever, so that breeders and farmers can draw on it when they need a trait that has vanished from the fields. The vault has already been used: seeds stored there were withdrawn to rebuild a seed bank in Lebanon after the original collection in Syria was damaged by war. The median is one of the five numbers, and statement II says it is even, so at least one of the five numbers is even, and the count of odd numbers cannot be 5. Either way there are at least two even numbers in S, and each even number contributes a factor of 2 to the product, so the product has at least two factors of 2 and is divisible by 4.
